analysis.one_liner: Bans for-profit prisons, caps prison phone fees, and ends immigration detention of families.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in four House committees from August 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with 20 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end federal use of for-profit prisons within two years and bar private companies from running state and local prisons or electronic monitoring of released people. It would cap jail and prison phone rates at 4 to 5 cents a minute, ban the 'site commissions' that phone companies pay to facilities, and put the consumer watchdog agency in charge of fees charged to move money to incarcerated people. It would also require humane treatment and independent inspection of immigration detention facilities, and replace detention of apprehended families with community-based case management run by nonprofits.
analysis.who_benefits: Incarcerated people and immigration detainees, and above all their families, who currently pay high phone and money-transfer fees to stay in touch and send funds. People held in immigration detention would get independent inspections and enforceable standards, and families picked up together could no longer be detained or separated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Incarcerated people, detainees, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Ends federal use of privately run prisons within two years, requiring all federal correctional facilities to be under direct government control with government employees performing core services, with a possible one-year waiver.

Bars private for-profit companies from owning or operating state and local prisons and detention alternatives after two years, and bans private companies from electronic monitoring of people released from custody.

Caps prison and jail phone calls at 4 cents a minute for debit or prepaid calls and 5 cents for collect calls, bans per-call connection fees, limits add-on fees, and prohibits the site commissions phone companies pay to facilities.

Directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules requiring that fees for transferring money to incarcerated people and immigration detainees be reasonable and proportional to the cost of the service.

Requires annual independent inspections of all immigration detention facilities, makes detention contracts and audits publicly available, imposes financial penalties on facilities that fail standards, and terminates contracts with repeat violators.
Prohibits detaining family units apprehended together and forbids separating them, replacing detention with community-based case management run by nonprofit organizations.
Gives individuals a private right of action to sue over violations, with damages of at least $1,000 per violation plus attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies, prison phone and video-call providers, money-transfer companies serving jails, and electronic-monitoring contractors would lose their business model. Some local governments that collect commissions from phone providers would lose that revenue, and governments would face transition costs in bringing facilities and services in-house.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison, jail phone, and money-transfer companies

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the Attorney General to waive the two-year phase-out for up to one more year at the federal level and per state or local facility, so full transition could stretch to three years.

It bans ankle-worn GPS trackers as an alternative to family detention, and no longer allows any detention of apprehended family units, leaving nonprofits' case management as the only mechanism for those cases.

Governments would take on the cost of running facilities and services currently handled by contractors, and local jails that rely on phone-company commissions for budget revenue would lose that income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to millions of incarcerated people, detainees, and their families, who today face some of the highest per-minute phone rates and steepest money-transfer fees in American consumer finance, and to detained families facing loss of liberty. The costs are real but transitional: governments must absorb facilities and services now run by contractors, and some jail budgets lose commission income. On balance the benefits substantially outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees in August 2020, then sent to two Homeland Security subcommittees, but no committee or subcommittee ever voted on it, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still parked in committee.

narrative.text: Representative Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on August 11, 2020, joined by 19 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
It was referred to the Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Homeland Security Committees; none of the four ever reported or voted on it.

In September 2020 it was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, and Operations and the Subcommittee on Oversight, Management, and Accountability, and no further action followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee, so it never reached the House or Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison companies and the jail phone and money-transfer industries, which kept their contracts and fee streams because the bill never advanced; House committees took no action on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison and jail telecom companies

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and with no vote ever held there was no floor test of either party's position.

industries.industry: Private prison and detention contractors (GEO Group, CoreCivic)
industries.note: The bill would end their federal contracts within two years and bar them from running state and local prisons, eliminating their core business of housing prisoners for profit. Ending profit-based detention removes incentives tied to filling beds and keeping people locked up.

industries.industry: Prison phone and video communications providers (Securus, Global Tel Link)
industries.note: Calls would be capped at 4 to 5 cents a minute, connection fees and most add-on charges banned, and the site commissions these companies pay to sheriffs and facilities outlawed. Families currently bear inflated rates that are partly driven by those commissions.

Their fees for moving money to incarcerated people and detainees would come under Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rules requiring fees proportional to actual cost. Families sending funds to loved ones are the direct consumers.

Private companies could no longer run ankle GPS monitoring of released people; only public agencies or nonprofits could. This ends a growing paid-surveillance business charged to people leaving custody.

industries.industry: Local governments receiving phone site commissions
industries.note: Jails and sheriffs' departments that collect commissions from phone providers would lose that revenue, though the same facilities benefit when their populations and families are not paying inflated rates.
The bill routes alternatives to family detention through community-based, community-supported programs operated by nonprofits, replacing detention beds with case management.
